bear.argument: KO's filing shows real pressure points a bear can press. Operating income rose 38% in 2025, but that jump was driven largely by lower other operating charges after a prior-year $3,109 million fairlife remeasurement; the filing itself notes 2025 operating income was hurt by an unfavorable currency impact of 12%. Unit case volume was flat at 33.8 billion cases, and North America volume fell 1%. Management warns that inflationary pressures on input costs will continue in 2026 and that price increases may reduce volume. The BodyArmor trademark took a $960 million impairment in 2025 on a slowing category outlook, with $2,440 million still carried, and the filing warns further impairments are likely if results disappoint. Most significantly, the IRS litigation exposes the company to roughly $14 billion of potential incremental tax and interest for 2010 through 2025, on top of the $6.0 billion already paid. Management is 'more likely than not' to prevail, but the filing concedes that outcome is not assured.

claims.claim: Flat volume and rising input-cost pressure threaten margins despite pricing
claims.quote: We expect the inflationary pressures on certain input and other costs to continue to impact our business in 2026.

claims.claim: A large contingent tax exposure remains beyond the amount already paid
claims.quote: The Company estimates that the potential aggregate remaining incremental tax and interest liability for the tax years 2010 through 2025 could be approximately $14 billion as of December 31, 2025.

claims.claim: Acquired brand impairments show acquisition value risk
claims.quote: If the near-term operating results of this trademark do not achieve our revised financial projections, or if the macroeconomic conditions change, causing the discount rate to increase without an offsetting increase in the operating results, it is likely that we would be required to recognize an additional impairment charge.

bull.argument: KO's 2025 filing shows a business that converts scale into cash and returns. Net operating revenues rose 2% to $47,941 million, with price/mix contributing 4% and gross profit margin widening to 61.6% from 61.1%. Operating income of $13,762 million was up 38%, and the filing ties the jump to pricing initiatives and volume growth, not only to lower charges. Operating cash flow grew 9% to $7,408 million, and the Company paid $8,779 million in dividends while guiding to a 64th consecutive annual dividend increase. Management says it is 'more likely than not' to prevail against the IRS, and it reports $15.8 billion in cash and short-term investments plus $6.2 billion in unused credit lines. Its credit ratings are A+ and A1. Pricing power, cash generation, and a long dividend record are the core of the case. The IRS exposure and the BodyArmor impairment are real, and the filing does disclose them, but the Company's liquidity is built to absorb them.

claims.claim: Pricing drove revenue growth and margin expansion
claims.quote: Our gross profit margin increased to 61.6% in 2025 from 61.1% in 2024.

claims.claim: Cash generation grew and funds dividends
claims.quote: Net cash provided by operating activities for the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024 was $7,408 million and $6,805 million, respectively, an increase of $603 million, or 9%.

claims.claim: Management views the IRS case favorably and liquidity is strong
claims.quote: While the Company believes that it is more likely than not that we will ultimately prevail in this litigation upon appeal

bear.argument: The bull case rests on figures the filing does support, but it omits what they cost. Operating income rose 38%, yet the filing attributes that jump primarily to lower other operating charges after a prior-year $3,109 million fairlife remeasurement, and it also cites an unfavorable currency impact of 12% on operating income. Price/mix of 4% did most of the work, while concentrate volume grew only 1% and unit case volume was even. Pricing that outruns volume depends on consumers accepting higher prices, which the risk factors warn may reduce volume. Operating cash flow of $7,408 million was helped by $6.1 billion of the $6.2 billion fairlife milestone, which is a one-time item, not a recurring trend. Dividends of $8,779 million exceeded operating cash flow. The filing's own liquidity language says the company can manage IRS outcomes only because it expects to borrow at reasonable rates, and it concedes the IRS could be 'upheld' in part, with about $14 billion of further exposure for 2010 through 2025. A 'more likely than not' view is not a guarantee.

claims.claim: Operating income growth was driven mainly by lower charges, not underlying growth
claims.quote: The increases in operating income and operating margin were primarily driven by lower other operating charges, due to the prior year remeasurement of our contingent consideration liability to fair value

claims.claim: Operating cash flow was boosted by a one-time fairlife payment
claims.quote: the activity in 2025 included $6.1 billion of the $6.2 billion final milestone payment for fairlife.

claims.claim: IRS outcome could still go against the company
claims.quote: it is possible that all, or some portion of, the adjustments proposed by the IRS and sustained by the Tax Court could ultimately be upheld.

bull.argument:
The bear is right that the 38% operating income jump was flattered by a prior-year $3,109 million fairlife remeasurement, so I will not present that growth as organic. But the filing's underlying pricing story is real: price/mix added 4% to revenue, and the cited drivers of operating income include 'favorable pricing initiatives' across every segment, with concentrate volume up 1%. Pricing and modest volume growth together, in a business with a 61.6% gross margin, is the profile of a company with pricing power rather than one buying growth. The risk factors describe the volume risk, but the filing reports volume grew in EMEA and Asia Pacific concentrate sales.

On cash, the bear is correct that the $6.1 billion fairlife payment sits in operating cash flow and makes the comparison noisy. That cuts both ways, since the 2024 base included the $6.0 billion IRS deposit. The dividend exceeding operating cash flow is a fair point, which is why the company also draws on $6.2 billion of unused credit lines and $15.8 billion of cash and investments. On the IRS, the filing does say the company believes it is more likely than not to prevail, and the $6.0 billion deposit is refundable if it does. The $14 billion figure is a disclosed range, not a judgment, and it is covered by the same liquidity the bear questions.

claims.claim: Pricing drove growth and margin expansion
claims.quote: Our gross profit margin increased to 61.6% in 2025 from 61.1% in 2024.

claims.claim: Price/mix was the main revenue driver
claims.quote: Price/mix had a 4% favorable impact on our consolidated net operating revenues.

claims.claim: Liquidity is backed by cash and credit lines
claims.quote: our ability to generate cash flows from operating activities and our ability to borrow funds at reasonable interest rates, we can manage the range of possible outcomes

judge.reasoning: All quotes in both sides verified, but the bear's evidence was more specific and better tied to the bull's claims: the bear showed the 38% operating income jump was driven by lower charges after a prior-year remeasurement, and that operating cash flow was flattered by a one-time fairlife payment. The bull conceded the first point and countered with price/mix and liquidity, but did not fully rebut the cash-flow distortion or the dividend exceeding operating cash flow, leaving the bear with the stronger rebuttal.
